timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Welcome to the Rossini College electronic series of videos. This video will be
about the discovery in early history of electricity and introducing some
fundamental concepts. In about 600 BC the Greeks realized that Amber, which is
fossilized tree sap, had some interesting properties. It could make our hair stand
up on end and pick up some light objects or in a generator spark if rubbed in a
certain way. Here is an example of a very large spark caused by the same
phenomenon that we now know as static electricity. It wasn't until the late
19th century that we started to really understand what was behind these
phenomena. JJ Thompson theorized that an atom consisted of two types of
particle, one positively charged and the other negatively charged. These were
spread evenly throughout the atom in what is known as the plum pudding model.
Anus Rutherford later performed experiments that showed this to be inaccurate,
beginning the development of the orbital model of the atom with a very small
positively charged and heavy nucleus and with negatively charged and light
particles called electrons in orbits around it. This is further developed by
Niels Bohr in the early 20th century, paving the way to our modern understanding of
the atom. Here is a much simplified diagram showing this. Charges are difficult
concept to describe well. However, it can be said that any charged particles will
feel the force of attraction or repulsion to another charged particle. Some
charges repel whereas some charges repel whereas opposite charges attract.
Charged particles have an electric field associated with them and more
formally it is the interaction of these fields that provide the forces we see.
Magnetism is also related to charged particles and we will explore this
further in another video. An electric current is where charged particles are
moving. In metals it is the electrons that move. Metals are different than
non-metals because some of the electrons in each atom become dissociated.
This means that these electrons do not belong to any one particular atom rather
they are shared between all metal atoms in their particular piece of metal.
They are known as D localised electrons and provide the metal with many of its
properties such as Luster or the shiny metallic look that we see. Malleability
which is ability to be bent or shaped without breaking or its ability and
more importantly for us it can conduct electricity as a solid. If a particle
with the excess charged is placed near a metal the electrons are repelled or
attracted depending on which charge it is and move accordingly. This has the
effect of containing the electric field associated with that particle
allowing us to use it. If electrons are continuously moving as in a circuit
we have an electric current you can think of it in similar terms to water moving
in a hose. I will be using the water analogy quite often to describe electricity
concepts however it should be noted that it does not always explain the whole
story. Next video I'll be looking at basic circuits and what current
voltage and resistance means in that context.
